\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{すな} (suna)}{すな (suna)}]{\ja{すな} (suna) — sand}

\label{lesson:JA-C43-suna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a forest, then the Japanese for a stone.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{すな}}
\textbf{\ja{すな}} — \emph{suna} — \textquotedblleft{}sand\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{すな}} (\emph{suna}) is a native Japanese word, inherited rather than borrowed from Chinese, and its older origin is not settled. Its kanji was attached to it later as a kun'yomi, a native reading given to a Chinese character (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{くも}}
\textbf{\ja{くも}} — \emph{kumo} — \textquotedblleft{}a cloud; a spider\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{くも}} (\emph{kumo}) is two native words that sound alike: \emph{kumo}, \textquotedblleft{}cloud\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{kumo}, \textquotedblleft{}spider\textquotedblright{}, each with its own kanji (JMdict). \end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{たいよう} (taiyou)}{たいよう (taiyou)}]{\ja{たいよう} (taiyou) — the sun}

\label{lesson:JA-C43-taiyou}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a star, then the Japanese for a cloud; a spider.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{たいよう}}
\textbf{\ja{たいよう}} — \emph{taiyou} — \textquotedblleft{}the sun\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{たいよう}} (\emph{taiyou}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{tai}, \textquotedblleft{}big, great\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{thajH}) and \emph{yō}, \textquotedblleft{}sun; the bright principle\textquotedblright{} (\emph{yang}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese in Baxter's transcription).
\end{cousinweb}
